raw_case_text:
A 37-year-old female presented to the emergency department with a 1-week history of progressive neck stiffness, severe headache, fever, and loss of weight. She reported no other neurological symptoms. She had no medical history of TB but was diagnosed with HIV two years ago. At a visit to her local clinic about 3 weeks before this admission, laboratory tests showed a CD4 cell count of 76 cells/muL. She was subsequently started on antiretroviral therapy:with tenofovir, emtricitabine, and efavirenz. Targeted screening for cryptococcal antigenemia was not yet offered by her clinic. The physical examination revealed tachycardia, pyrexia, conjunctival pallor, and generalized lymphadenopathy. Neck stiffness was present, but no confusion, focal neurologic deficit, papilledema, or cranial nerve involvement was evident on neurological examination. No pulmonary or dermatological changes were noted. The remainder of the systemic examination was otherwise normal.
The initial CSF opening pressure was raised (28 cm H20). CSF was clear in appearance, and further analysis revealed lymphocytes of 34 cells/muL, neutrophils of 5 cells/muL, protein of 1.83 g/dL (normal: 0.15-0.45 g/dL), and glucose of 1.9 mmol/L (normal: 2.8-4.4 mmol/L). Gram's stain of the CSF was negative. The cryptococcal latex antigen test (CLAT) and India ink were, however, positive. CSF CrAg titres are not routinely performed in South Africa, as antifungal treatment is standardised and fungal burden at the time of diagnosis is invariably high. Other laboratory tests showed a positive peripheral blood CrAg LFA and a normocytic anaemia (haemoglobin: 9.2 g/L). Chest radiography was normal.
A diagnosis was made of cryptococcal meningitis with raised intracranial pressure and unmasking HIV-associated IRIS. ART was continued in the ward, and antifungal therapy was started with amphotericin B (1 mg/kg/day IV) and high dose fluconazole of 800 mg daily. Fluconazole is used in South Africa, as flucytosine is presently unavailable. Intravenous antimicrobial therapy with ceftriaxone was also started. To avoid nephrotoxicity and electrolyte abnormalities, she was prehydrated and given potassium and magnesium supplements. No nephrotoxicity or worsening of anaemia was noted during admission. Therapeutic lumbar puncture was performed three times a week to relieve symptoms of raised intracranial pressure, and paracetamol was given for further analgesia. Corticosteroids were also added to the regimen. By hospital day 14, her symptoms had improved greatly. Intravenous amphotericin was stopped and the dose of fluconazole was changed to 400 mg daily. She was discharged from hospital 3 weeks after admission. At her 2-month follow-up visit, she was maintained on fluconazole of 200 mg daily as secondary prophylaxis. She is currently well and reports no recurrence of her symptoms.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 37-year-old female presenting with a 1-week history of severe headache, progressive neck stiffness, fever, and weight loss.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient developed worsening severe headaches, progressive neck stiffness, fever, and involuntary weight loss over a 1-week period, approximately two weeks after initiating combination antiretroviral therapy. She reported no focal neurological deficits, visual changes, or seizures.
subjective.past_medical_history: Chronic retroviral infection diagnosed 2 years prior; initiated on antiretroviral therapy (tenofovir, emtricitabine, efavirenz) 3 weeks prior when CD4 cell count was 76 cells/mcL. No prior history of tuberculosis.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for severe holocephalic headache, neck stiffness, pyrexia, and weight loss; negative for visual loss, confusion, nausea, vomiting, cough, or dyspnea. Home medications: tenofovir, emtricitabine, efavirenz. Allergies: unmentioned.

objective.physical_examination: Vital signs: tachycardia, pyrexia/fever. General: conjunctival pallor, generalized lymphadenopathy. Neurologic: prominent neck stiffness / nuchal rigidity; alert, oriented, no confusion; no papilledema; cranial nerves intact; no focal motor or sensory deficits. Lungs and skin: clear, no cutaneous or pulmonary findings.
objective.routine_investigations: Complete blood count: normocytic anemia with hemoglobin 9.2 g/dL (transcribed 9.2 g/L). Chest radiograph: normal.
objective.advanced_workup: Lumbar puncture: opening pressure elevated at 28 cm H2O; CSF clear; lymphocytes: 34 cells/mcL, neutrophils: 5 cells/mcL, protein elevated at 1.83 g/dL (normal: 0.15-0.45 g/dL), glucose depressed at 1.9 mmol/L (normal: 2.8-4.4 mmol/L); CSF Gram stain: negative.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Definitive diagnosis: Cryptococcal meningitis with intracranial hypertension secondary to unmasking immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome (IRIS) in advanced human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) / AIDS (baseline CD4 count 76 cells/mcL). Confirmed by positive cerebrospinal fluid India ink examination, positive CSF cryptococcal latex antigen test (CLAT), and positive serum cryptococcal antigen lateral flow assay (CrAg LFA). Bacterial meningitis ruled out by negative Gram stain. Management & Outcome: Continued on antiretroviral therapy; treated with intravenous amphotericin B (1 mg/kg/day) plus high-dose oral fluconazole (800 mg daily) and empiric IV ceftriaxone, accompanied by prehydration and electrolyte supplementation (potassium and magnesium). Systemic corticosteroids were added for IRIS. Raised intracranial pressure was managed with serial therapeutic lumbar punctures three times weekly and paracetamol. Marked clinical improvement achieved by day 14, allowing discontinuation of amphotericin B and transition to oral fluconazole 400 mg daily. Discharged after 3 weeks, and maintained on fluconazole 200 mg daily secondary prophylaxis at 2-month follow-up without symptom relapse.
